observed: Daily research turned up two design corrections and one fatal caveat for volatility harvesting, the most disruptive idea in the catalogue. Under proportional transaction costs the optimal rule is MOVE-based, not time-based, so the queued design was wrong. And the premium depends on DISPERSION rather than volatility - if assets are highly correlated they never outgrow one another and there is nothing to trim. Measuring that precondition on our own universe rather than trusting either the idea or the caveat: an equal-weight basket rebalanced with the real toll is positive in only two of seven years, with medians of -5.8% weekly, -4.5% monthly and -2.2% on a 5% band, and it is NEGATIVE in both years that matter - about -2% in 2022 and -36% to -45% in 2025. Average pairwise correlation runs 0.47 to 0.69.
decided: Kill A50 before building it. The mechanism is real, the literature is right about it, and this universe simply fails its precondition: correlated crypto rarely oscillates around itself, one name persistently leads, and rebalancing then sells the leader to buy laggards - a drag rather than a harvest, costing 175 points in 2021 at its worst. The tolerance band was least-bad, exactly as the theory predicts for proportional costs, but least-bad is still negative. observed: With P09 on its final arm, I tested a claim I had already given the operator as fact: that the selection law - worst year plus a tenth of CAGR - was one of two reasons the book runs at under one percent of capital. Re-scoring 153 stored risk-grid sweeps under weights of 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 1.00 and 2.00 costs nothing, since it is the same measured per-year returns scored a different way. Multiplying the weight TWENTYFOLD moves median CAGR only from +21.2% to +28.3%, degrades the median worst year from -8.4% to -13.1%, and never once selects a configuration other than two positions at fraction 0.15 - the only thing that moves is the deployment ceiling, from 0.35 to 0.5, which is the largest value the grid contains. At weight 0.25 the choice is identical in 97% of iterations.

The law does steer - at weight 2.00 it picks a different row in 37% of iterations - but it can only choose among rows that all deploy a tiny amount, so no weight produces a large book from this menu. The practical consequence is that changing the CAGR weight is a real choice about how much yearly profit is worth against a bad year, and it will NOT on its own answer his complaint, because the option he wants was never on the ballot. Widening the grid is the change that matters, which is exactly what P09 measures by taking the ceiling past 0.5 for the first time. observed: Before widening the grid on P09's evidence I checked an obvious objection: the grid ALREADY contains a row with regime_deploy 0.5, so why did P09 measure an improvement? Because regime.py computes deployment two different ways. With regime_persist above zero it uses deploy = max(0.05, regime_deploy * smoothed_score), where position_fraction plays no part; with persist at zero it uses deploy = position_fraction + (regime_deploy - position_fraction) * score, where position_fraction is the floor. The grid's only 0.5 row carries persist 480 and so uses the first formula, while the champion runs the second at a 0.35 ceiling, and nine of eleven rows are 0.35. The configuration P09 measured has never existed in the grid.
